source.title: Optical Transformers
source.authors: Maxwell G. Anderson; Shi-Fan Ma; Tian-Yu Wang; L. Wright; P. McMahon

record.tranche_reason: The study reports language-model performance as optical photon usage changes, but does not test the claim’s loss scaling with parameter count, training tokens, or compute, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It discusses deriving distinct scaling tradeoffs for optical systems as future work.
record.gate_note: The paper’s own optical-scaling results concern validation perplexity and the photon budget, not the claim’s stated scaling variables. Those adjacent results are recorded under fits_no_version. Citations to prior language-model scaling work are not results from this study. The precision ablation is not a test of the claim.
record.test_reason: The study's scaling results concern simulated optical Transformers. They relate validation perplexity to photon budget per MAC, and the photons needed to match 8-bit digital perplexity to width d. None of its results relate held-out loss to parameters, tokens or compute, test extrapolation, fit a compute-optimal split, vary model shape at fixed size, or measure downstream scaling. Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are cited only as background. Deriving optical-hardware scaling laws is named as future work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is partly right but misses the headline conclusion. Simulations, validated by small optical experiments, show optical energy per MAC scaling as 1/d. The authors project about a 100x energy advantage over A100-class GPUs for the largest current models, and over 8000x for hypothetical quadrillion-parameter models. They note that photon efficiency depends on the training and quantization scheme, and leave optical-specific model scaling laws to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates optical photon usage and simulated optical execution of Wikitext-103 Transformers; it does not fit the original parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling laws or optimize the parameter/token split.
record.method_sensitivity: Photon efficiency changes with training and quantization scheme: Appendix H reports different photon requirements under percentile clipping versus EMA-statistics clamping, and inconsistent scaling under percentile clipping.

fits_no_version.finding: Percent perplexity degradation from the 10K photons/MAC level follows a truncated power law in photons/MAC for all four model widths (Fig. 4 middle, Fig. 13 middle).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optical-inference perplexity degradation follows a truncated power law in photon budget per MAC.

fits_no_version.finding: With EMA clamping, the photons needed to match 8-bit digital perplexity fall nearly as 1/d. With percentile clipping this scaling is inconsistent: fewer photons for small models (120 and 40 vs 340 and 170), but poor efficiency for the largest model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Photon-efficiency scaling of optical Transformers with width depends on the quantization/training scheme.

record.problems: The optical scaling results are simulations rather than full-model optical experiments; the physical setup sampled dot products from a base-sized model only. The simulated models range from 15M to 416.3M non-embedding parameters, and the text identifies training and quantization choices as affecting photon efficiency.

untested.parts: No fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Only four widths, trained for a fixed 90k steps on Wikitext-103.
Depth is fixed at 12 layers. Shape is not varied at a fixed parameter count.
No other modality or regime tested for parameter/data/compute scaling.
Fitting-choice dependence is shown only for photon-efficiency trends, not for loss-scaling exponents.

record.verdict_notes: 'Scaling laws' in this paper means performance versus optical energy/photon usage, not the claim's loss scaling. Figure 4 left plots perplexity against width for four models, but no power-law fit in parameters is reported, and training length is fixed at 90k steps, so it cannot test V1. The Table 5 precision ablation (val. loss versus bit precision) is likewise unrelated to any version.
